- entire:teach: Use when a developer wants a topic-focused guided lesson built from canonical checkpoints, not a whole-repo overview. Triggers on phrases like "teach me <topic>", "teach me how this repo handles", "how does <topic> work in this repo", "give me a lesson on", "school me on", and "I need to learn about"
- entire:using-entire: Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
- entire:what-happened: Explain why code looks the way it does by tracing the latest change for a file range or pasted snippet through `git blame` and deduplicated `entire explain` lookups. Use when the user asks what happened, says "tell me why" about a code block, is confused about a section of code, asks "wtf is going on", "why is this like this", "why was this changed", or wants provenance for a specific file block.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# DevDesk Backlog
2	
3	**Last Updated:** 2026-08-03
4	
5	Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
6	Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
7	(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
8	rather than carried over.
9	
10	---
11	
12	## 1. Known defects
13	
14	**Three open**, all in the registry browser and all found while reviewing the
15	design for §3.8 rather than by a test. See [§1.3](#13-open). D1–D11 and D15–D19
16	are fixed; §1.1 records what each was and why the chosen fix was the right one.
17	
18	The five that stayed open longest — D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 — were parked not
19	because they were hard but because each altered something the user already saw,
20	so they needed a deliberate call rather than a drive-by fix. All five were then
21	decided together and fixed in one pass; see [§1.2](#12-the-five-parked-defects).
22	
23	### 1.1 Fixed
24	
25	**The command line took focus from the render path.** Found in phase 5.
26	`renderHeader` called `a.commandInput.Focus()` whenever `commandMode` was set —
27	a mutation inside `View()`, which Rule 110 makes read-only. A
28	`bubbles/textinput` drops every key it receives while blurred, so the command
29	line only accepted typing because a render happened to have run first. Focus is
30	now taken in `enterCommandMode` and released alongside the existing `Blur()`
31	calls on the way out. In production the ordering held, so nothing was visibly
32	broken; the coupling surfaced the moment a test drove the router without
33	rendering, and the same latent bug would bite anyone reordering the loop.
34	
35	**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
36	phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.
37	
38	The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
39	the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
40	was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
41	The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
42	without documenting it at all.
43	
44	The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
45	where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
46	stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.
47	
48	`explorer` made it four in a row, though only just: every key was documented
49	except `/`. The check caught it on its first run.
50	
51	`security` broke the streak — its help documents every key its header
52	advertises, across all four states.
53	
54	`oci_resources` then produced the worst instance, in phase 4. The Networks and
55	Volumes tabs documented `n` for a binding that has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111
56	renamed it — the same drift `status` and `workspaces` carried — but the **whole
57	Registries tab was undocumented**: `ctrl+n`, `e`, `l` and `L` appeared nowhere,
58	so four actions on a tab were reachable only by guessing.
59	
60	That view needed one adjustment to the check: its help qualifies most keys with
61	the tab they belong to (`enter (Images)`, `ctrl+n (Networks)`), so the
62	parenthetical comes off before matching. That convention is worth keeping — with
63	four tabs sharing a keymap, an unqualified `enter` would be ambiguous.
64	
65	So the pattern across five views: the drift is a Rule 111 rename the help did
66	not follow, plus whole surfaces added later and never documented at all.
67	
68	All five are fixed, and every view in `internal/ui` now asserts that each key
69	`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
70	have caught the drift when it was introduced.
71	
72	**The explorer acted on a different row than the one highlighted.** Found in
73	phase 3, and the most serious defect the coverage work has turned up.
74	
75	`handleKeyMsg` resolved the cursor against `sortedItems(currentItems())` — the
76	unfiltered list — while the table was built from the filtered one. With a filter
77	active the two indices disagree, so `ctrl+d`, `p`, `→` and `ctrl+w` all acted on
78	whatever happened to sit at that index in the *unfiltered* list. Filtering to a
79	single project and pressing `ctrl+d` scheduled a different group for deletion.
80	`GetShortcuts` had it too, so even the advertised `ctrl+w` keyed off the wrong
81	node.
82	
83	Both now go through `visibleItems()`, the single list `updateTableRows` builds
84	from. Pinned by `TestActionsResolveTheRowTheUserCanSee`, which filters to a row
85	that sits at a different index in each list — the fixtures were chosen so the
86	two cannot coincide.
87	
88	**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
89	clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
90	fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
91	highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
92	until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.
93	
94	The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
95	change; workspaces had no equivalent. **`explorer` had it too**, and only on the
96	filter path — its drill-down was already safe because it calls `GotoTop()`.
97	Fixed the same way.
98	
99	**Two tabs reported nothing when Docker was down.** Found in phase 4.
100	`handleImagesList` has always set a footer message on failure;
101	`handleNetworksList` and `handleVolumesList` only logged, so with the daemon
102	stopped those two tabs showed an empty table — indistinguishable from "you have
103	no networks". Both now match their sibling.
104	
105	**The Registries tab opened empty.** `switchTab` focused the table and fired the
106	`docker login` status check, but never called `updateRegistryTable()` — so the
107	tab stayed blank until an asynchronous Docker call answered, even though the
108	registries come from the config file and were available immediately.
109	
110	**A search counter with no floor.** `RegistryBrowser.AddRegistryTags`
111	decremented `pendingSearches` unconditionally. A duplicate or late response drove
112	it negative, and the *next* search then started from that base: `IsSearching()`
113	stayed false while requests were genuinely in flight, so the spinner never
114	showed. Floored at zero.
115	
116	**Footer messages with no timer.** `explorer.handleDeleteComplete` set
117	`footerError` and returned `nil`, so a failed delete left "Delete failed — check
118	logs" on screen until something else overwrote it. Rule 128 caps footer messages
119	at three seconds, and the same file's `BrowserOpenedMsg` handler already did it
120	correctly. Now returns `clearFooterErrorCmd()`.
121	
122	The security view had it worse: **Rule 128 was not honoured anywhere in it.**
123	`statusMessage` was set in three places — "Added x to .gitleaksignore", "Failed
124	to ignore secret", "No references available" — and there was no clear timer in
125	the package at all, so whichever happened last stayed on screen until a tab
126	switch happened to reset it. `clearStatusCmd` / `clearStatusMsg` added and all
127	three wired, pinned by `TestFooterMessagesExpire`.
128	
129	**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
130	"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
131	unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
132	independent defects with no shared code.
133	
134	`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
135	normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
136	Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
137	`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
138	silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
139	(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
140	first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
141	that treats it as one.
142	
143	The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
144	`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
145	navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
146	line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
147	confusing than one that is plainly not there.
148	
149	The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
150	cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
151	was guarding.
152	
153	Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
154	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
155	`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
156	confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
157	`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
158	alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.
159	
160	**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
161	looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
162	fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.
163	
164	Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
165	`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
166	the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
167	terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
168	ones.
169	
170	A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
171	in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
172	Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
173	gone.
174	
175	A **sixth site** closed the family out, in the last package of phase 3:
176	`parseVersion` in `internal/ui/security` truncated its fallback with
177	`result[:15]`. Version strings are ASCII in practice, so this was the
178	lowest-risk of the six — but it is the same pattern, and it is now
179	`theme.TruncateWidth`. Grepping for `[:` on strings across `internal/ui` now
180	returns nothing but slice indexing.
181	
182	The same function had a second defect: it scanned for the version number by
183	taking the first whitespace-separated token starting with `v`, so
184	`gitleaks version 8.18.2` reported its version as **"version"**. A leading `v`
185	now only counts when a digit follows it.
186	
187	A **fifth site** turned up during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
188	`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
189	results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
190	could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
191	`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
192	Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.
193	
194	The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
195	(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
196	`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).
197	
198	One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
199	`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
200	so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
201	theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.
202	
203	**Every scan came back empty.** Introduced by the `internal/scan` split itself
204	and caught within the hour by the coverage pass that followed it — the clearest
205	argument yet for the surface → split → cover order.
206	
207	Extracting the subprocess seam collapsed two statements into one return:
208	
209	```go
210	return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(tc.Name, cmd.Wait(), stderr.String())
211	```
212	
213	Operands are evaluated before the call, so `stdout.Bytes()` snapshots the buffer
214	**before** `cmd.Wait()` runs — and `os/exec` fills that buffer from goroutines
215	only Wait is guaranteed to have finished. `Bytes()` returns a slice header with
216	the length at that moment, so later writes are invisible: the report was always
217	empty, every scan reported no findings, and the exit code alone survived. The
218	code it replaced got this right by accident of being written as separate
219	statements.
220	
221	The read now lives in `finish`, after Wait, with the reasoning recorded next to
222	it so it is not re-collapsed. Pinned by `TestTheReportOnStdoutIsWhatComesBack`,
223	which is the test that failed first when the seam was finally exercised.
224	
225	Worth stating plainly: this is the one defect in this list that the tests
226	*introduced* rather than merely found, and it never reached a commit. A
227	mechanical-looking refactor changed evaluation order, which is exactly what a
228	package with no tests under it cannot tell you.
229	
230	**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
231	planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.
232	
233	The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
234	credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
235	unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
236	credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
237	same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
238	won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
239	after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
240	strips the path before the helper is ever called.
241	
242	**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
243	the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
244	change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
245	`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.
246	
247	Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
248	path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
249	contexts anyway.
250	
251	Two smaller defects went with it:
252	
253	- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
254	  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
255	  hang indefinitely.
256	- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
257	  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
258	  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
259	  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.
260	
261	`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
262	than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
263	`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
264	common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
265	`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
266	`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.
267	
268	**D15 — `esc` never reached a view that was not editing.** The router answered
269	`esc` itself through `maybeQuitCommandMode`, forwarding it only when the view
270	reported `InEditMode()`. Every esc-to-go-back handler behind that gate was dead
271	code: the explorer's `esc` → `handleDrillUp` could not fire, though Rule 111
272	lists `esc` as the third way up.
273	
274	**Fix:** the router no longer names `esc` at all — it falls through to the
275	default branch and is forwarded like any other key. What made this smaller than
276	it looked is that the router had nothing left to do with `esc` by the time the
277	branch ran: `handleCommandMode` answers first whenever the command line is open,
278	so `maybeQuitCommandMode` was resetting an already-closed line and asking for a
279	redundant resize. It is deleted.
280	
281	The interesting half is what the gate had done to the views. Two of them
282	declared themselves *editing* in states holding no field at all, for one reason
283	— it was the only way to be handed `esc`. The security view said so outright:
284	`InEditMode()` was documented as *"returns true when the view needs to handle
285	ESC key"*, and claimed `StateScanning`, `StateResults` and `StateDetails`;
286	netdiag claimed `StateRunning` and `StateDetails`. That claim costs more than it
287	buys, because `InEditMode()` also governs `:`, `q` and `?` — so the security
288	results screen, the one place a user most wants to jump elsewhere, was the one
289	place `:` did nothing. Both predicates are now about focus and nothing else, and
290	those states get the command line, the help overlay and quit back.
291	
292	Left alone deliberately: the containers view claims `stateLogs`, where `q`
293	really is the view's own key for leaving the log pane. That is key ownership,
294	not a workaround for `esc`.
295	
296	**D16 — `:netdiag` was documented but not accepted.** One missing map entry.
297	**D17 — the completion catalogue was a subset of the parser.** Eight commands
298	listed against fourteen views plus aliases, kept by hand in two places.
299	
300	**Fix, for both:** one map. `viewNames` in `parser.go` maps every accepted
301	spelling to its view, the key equal to the `ViewType` being the full name and
302	every other key an alias; `GetAliases()` and the new `FullNames()` derive from
303	it, and the completion engine derives from those. Two tests hold the two ends
304	together — everything the parser accepts is suggested, everything suggested
305	parses — so the lists cannot drift apart again. `ParseCommand` lost its chain of
306	`if mainCmd ==` comparisons to the same treatment, `actionNames` and
307	`actionAliases`, and `Parse` is now a lookup in `viewNames` rather than a third
308	copy of it.
309	
310	Two aliases documented in `CLAUDE.md` but accepted nowhere came out of this —
311	`gle` for the explorer and `w` for workspaces — the same defect as D16, found by
312	the test rather than by reading. `ViewNet` was renamed `ViewNetdiag` and its
313	value changed from `net` to `netdiag`, so the full name matches the view, the
314	package and the documentation; `net` remains an alias.
315	
316	**D18 — the header overflowed a narrow window.** `buildShortcutLines` meant to
317	clip the shortcut block to its column — the comment said *"Truncate if wider
318	than col2Width"* — but called `theme.PadWithBg`, which returns content untouched
319	once it is already at or past the target. Below roughly 100 columns the header
320	rendered wider than the window and wrapped, costing the viewport a row.
321	
322	**Fix:** `lipgloss.NewStyle().MaxWidth(col2Width)`, which truncates on rune
323	boundaries without cutting an escape sequence in half — the corruption Rule 122
324	is about. Width 80 is now part of `TestEveryHeaderRowFillsTheWidth`, and a
325	second test checks no row ends inside an escape sequence, which is the failure a
326	naive slice would have produced.
327	
328	### 1.2 The five parked defects
329	
330	D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 were each recorded rather than fixed on discovery,
331	because each changed something the user already saw. They were decided together
332	and fixed in one pass. Three of the five had a test written to fail *on the
333	fix*, and all three did.
334	
335	**D4 — `tab` navigated the delete confirmation.** Rule 135 reserves `tab` for
336	switching tabs and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively; the modal
337	had it exactly inverted, cycling on `tab` and clamping on `↑ / ↓`. `↑ / ↓` now
338	cycle, which is what keeps every control reachable in one direction, and the
339	`tab` cases are gone. The explorer no longer advertises "tab Navigate" while the
340	modal is open, and `↑↓` is not advertised in its place — Rule 138 calls it
341	obvious. The permanent variant still skips its locked checkbox, so cycling there
342	toggles between the two buttons.
343	
344	**D8 — write-only CRUD flags.** `creating`, `editing` and `confirming` were
345	assigned in five places and read in none, and `ComponentFormCancelledMsg` — the
346	only thing that would have reset two of them — could never be sent. Deleted, all
347	of it. Nothing else changed: the phase 2 tests had deliberately asserted on
348	`componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags, which is what made
349	this safe a phase later.
350	
351	**D9 — the containers list opened Z→A.** `New()` set neither `sortColumn` nor
352	`sortAsc`, so both took their zero value. Both are now set explicitly, so the
353	default is stated rather than inherited. `TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending`
354	became `TestDefaultSortIsNameAscending`, and the cycle test walks forward from
355	ascending. The `loadedModel` helper still sets the sort itself even though it
356	now matches the constructor: those tests should say which order they rely on.
357	
358	**D10 — a registry failure was invisible.** `renderTemplateList` returned early
359	when the field was unfocused and the warning sat below that return, so a form
360	opened after the OCI registry failed offered a Template field reading "none"
361	with nothing to distinguish "the registry is down" from "there are no
362	templates". The warning moved into `renderTemplateWarning` and is appended in
363	both branches — it explains why the list is empty, so it belongs wherever the
364	list is.
365	
366	**D11 — CRITICAL and HIGH rendered identically.** `getSeverityStyle` composed
367	CRITICAL by hand as `ColorError` + `Bold`, which is byte-for-byte the
368	`theme.StatusErrorStyle` it returned for HIGH. The palette moved to
369	`theme.SeverityTextStyle`, next to the `TableStylesForSeverity` it draws from,
370	and the view delegates (Rule 102). An unrecognised severity now falls back to
371	the info colour rather than to `DimStyle`, so it is still legible.
372	
373	The pattern worth keeping: when a defect is recorded rather than fixed, write
374	the test **inverted** — asserting the current behaviour and saying so. D9, D10
375	and D11 each had one, and each failed the moment the fix landed, which is how
376	the stale test and the stale backlog entry got found together.
377	
378	### 1.3 Open
379	
380	D12–D14 sit in `internal/ui/oci_resources` and are cheap on their own, but
381	§3.8 rewrites the code path each of them lives in. Fix them **as part of** that
382	work rather than ahead of it, and write each one's test inverted first, per the
383	pattern above.
384	
385	D15–D19 were found by the phase 5 pass, were unrelated to §3.8, and are fixed —
386	see §1.1. Each had been recorded with an inverted test asserting the broken
387	behaviour; those tests are what failed when the fix landed, and each has been
388	turned around to assert the fixed behaviour instead.
389	
390	**D12 — `AuthEnabled` has no effect on browse or discovery.** The flag is
391	honoured in exactly three places: the `docker login` fired on form submit, the
392	`Logged` column, and the URL list `registryLoginStatusCmd` checks. Neither code
393	path that actually talks to a registry consults it. `submitSearch`
394	(`browser_keys.go:142`) calls `docker.GetStoredCreds(credURL)`
395	unconditionally and hands the result to `searchRegistryTagsCmd`;
396	`detectRegistryGroupCmd` (`commands.go:563`) does the same before calling into
397	`registrymgr`. A registry the user has marked as needing no authentication will
398	still have the host's stored credentials sent to it whenever any other registry
399	on that host has been logged into — which, given that Docker keys credentials by
400	host, is the normal case for a Nexus instance. This is the defect the
401	`anonymous` mode in §3.8 exists to make expressible; today there is no way to
402	say "do not send credentials here" at all.
403	
404	**D13 — the browser cannot be dismissed while it is resolving.**
405	`handleKeyMsg` returns `nil` for every key in `browserStateResolving`
406	(`browser_keys.go:70`), `esc` included, and that state is entered
407	unconditionally on open whenever any registry is configured. The detections run
408	concurrently with an 8 s timeout each, so the wedge is bounded at roughly eight
409	seconds — but it is eight seconds during which the application ignores the user,
410	on a screen they may have opened by mistake. §3.8 removes the state rather than
411	the symptom: with members read from config and cache, there is nothing to
412	resolve and the form renders immediately.
413	
414	A smaller thing in the same handler, not worth its own entry:
415	`HandleGroupDetected` matches the incoming result against `reg.URL`, so two
416	registries configured with the same URL collide and the second result overwrites
417	the first. The slug introduced in §3.8 is the natural key to match on instead.
418	
419	**D14 — the registry filter shows a raw URL for group members.**
420	`registryFilterLabel()` (`browser_tags.go:63`) resolves the active filter by
421	searching `b.registries`, which holds only the configured top-level entries.
422	Discovered members are not in that list, so filtering to one falls through to
423	returning `b.registryFilter` — the full synthesised URL — where every other row
424	in the same view shows a short alias. The fix follows from §3.8 rather than
425	preceding it: once members are persisted they are resolvable, and the filter
426	gains a group level at the same time.

734	### Race detector cannot run locally
735	
736	`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
737	it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
738	concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.
739	
740	**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
741	every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
742	run reported no data race across all 17 packages.
743	
744	That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
745	tests actually execute, and coverage is 73.6 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
746	paths remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so this is an argument for the
747	coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.
748	
749	`internal/scan` is the package the detector has most to say about, since
750	`Scanner.Scan` is the only place in the application that fans out to concurrent
751	goroutines writing one shared result. Its tests now drive all five stages at
752	once, so that fan-out is under the detector for the first time — but only on CI,
753	which is where the confirmation has to be read.
754	
755	Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
756	avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.

842	| `parser.go:120` `commands` | `Parse()`, legacy, duplicates the above |
843	| `parser.go:155` `GetAliases()` | feeds completion |
844	| `completion.go:47` `buildCommands` | a fourth hardcoded list, **stale today** |
845	
846	`buildCommands` offers `gitlab-auth` but not `gitlab-explorer`, and omits
847	`workspaces`, `security` and `net` entirely — so those commands work but are
848	never suggested. Adding a forge dimension to four unsynchronised tables
849	guarantees the drift gets worse. **Collapsing them to one source table is a
850	prerequisite**, and it is worth doing on its own: it fixes the stale completion
851	list today, independently of GitHub.
852	
853	#### Model mismatches to settle before coding
854	
855	These are not implementation details; they decide what the abstraction can even
856	promise.
857	
858	- **Nesting — settled.** The explorer is a tree of groups → subgroups →
859	  projects. GitHub has no nested groups, but it does have **organisations**, and
860	  a user can belong to several. Flattening everything to one level was
861	  considered and rejected: someone in five orgs would get a wall of repositories
862	  with no way to tell them apart by owner. The abstraction therefore **declares
863	  its depth** — `MaxDepth: 1` for GitHub (orgs at level 1, repositories at level
864	  2), unbounded for GitLab. This costs nothing in the UI: the drill-down already
865	  handles two levels, and a user with no organisation simply sees a flat list.
866	- **Deletion.** `DeleteGroup` / `DeleteProject` implement GitLab's two-step
867	  permanent delete (schedule, then purge under the renamed
868	  `-deletion_scheduled-<id>` path). GitHub deletes immediately and has no
869	  equivalent, so the "permanent" checkbox is meaningless there. The `locked`
870	  flag added in §1.1 is the hook for that: a GitHub backend would set it and
871	  leave the box out of reach, as the already-scheduled GitLab case does.
872	- **Dashboard counters.** `FetchDashboardStats` reads `X-Total` from five list
873	  endpoints. GitHub has no equivalent header for these; the counts come from the
874	  search API (`search/issues?q=is:open+is:pr+assignee:@me`), with different rate
875	  limits and semantics.
876	- **Vocabulary.** Group/project/merge request vs organisation/repository/pull
877	  request. The UI must pick per-backend labels or a neutral vocabulary; Rule 129
878	  applies either way.
879	
880	#### Settled: vocabulary, commands and forge selection
881	
882	The organising distinction, which the mismatches above blur: the two forges
883	differ in **words** and in **shapes**, and only the first is a presentation
884	problem.
885	
886	| Difference | Kind | Handled by |
887	|---|---|---|
888	| "Group" vs "Organization" | word | vocabulary table |
889	| "Merge Request" vs "Pull Request" | word | vocabulary table |
890	| Token label, placeholder, help URL | word | vocabulary table |
891	| Icon and display name | word | vocabulary table |
892	| Nested namespaces | **shape** | declared depth (above) |
893	| Visibility set — 3 values vs 2 | **shape** | forge-supplied option list |
894	| Role model — int levels vs strings | **shape** | backend returns a humanised role |
895	| Two-step permanent delete | **shape** | the `locked` flag, §1.1 |
896	| Dashboard counters | **shape** | different endpoints, above |
897	
898	Words are cheap and settle in one pass. Shapes are the actual work, and neither
899	neutral nor per-forge wording helps with them. Keeping the two apart is what
900	stops the vocabulary layer from quietly growing conditionals.
901	
902	**Vocabulary is per-forge, not neutral.** A GitLab user says *group*, a GitHub
903	user says *repository*; "namespace" is a third language nobody speaks, and it
904	makes the application read as an abstraction layer rather than a tool. The
905	wording lives in a single `Vocabulary` value per forge — name, icon, namespace
906	singular/plural, repository, change-request, token label and placeholder, help
907	URL, visibility set, role names — resolved once from the active context and
908	carried on `shared.State`, which every view already receives.
909	
910	The rule that keeps it maintainable: **no view interpolates a forge name into a
911	string literal.** That is enforceable the way this project already pins
912	invariants — a test grepping `internal/ui` for `"GitLab"` / `"GitHub"`, on the
913	model of the existing check that every key in `GetShortcuts()` appears in
914	`GetHelpContent()`.
915	
916	Sites to move, none of them subtle:
917	
918	| Location | Literal |
919	|---|---|
920	| `explorer/view.go:342` | `IconGitlab + " GitLab Explorer"` |
921	| `explorer/view.go:258` | `"GitLab not authenticated … with :gitlab-auth (or :gla)"` — name **and** command |
922	| `explorer/view.go:267` | `"No groups found … any GitLab groups."` |
923	| `explorer/view.go:81` | `"Loading GitLab groups..."` |
924	| `explorer/view.go:210` | `nodeTypeLabel()` → `"Group"` / `"Project"` |
925	| `components/creation_form.go:26` | `resourceTypes = []string{"Group", "Project"}` |
926	| `auth/view.go:46` | `IconUser + " Gitlab Authentication"` — wrong icon *and* wrong casing next to the explorer's |
927	| `auth/view.go:132,140` | `"GitLab URL"`, `"Personal Access Token"` |
928	| `auth/view.go:81` | help text asserting the token starts with `glpat-` |
929	| `dashboard/view.go:80,85` | `IconGitlab + " GitLab"`, `"Authenticate with :gitlab-auth"` |
930	| `dashboard/view.go:104` | `"Merge Requests:"` |
931	
932	Two of these are shapes wearing a word's clothes. `AccessLevelName()`
933	(`tree.go:52`) maps GitLab's numeric levels to Owner/Maintainer/…; GitHub uses
934	`admin`/`maintain`/`push`/`triage`/`pull`, which do not align one-to-one — so the
935	**backend returns an already-humanised role string** rather than an integer the
936	UI translates. And `internal` visibility does not exist on GitHub.com, so
937	`CreationForm`'s three hardcoded values have to come from the forge. Nothing to
938	undo for the token prefix: `glpat-` appears only in help text, never validated.
939	
940	**Routing identity is forge-neutral; only aliases and titles vary.** `ViewType`
941	is a map key in `a.views` and a `switch` case in `app.go:1480,1496`, so it stays
942	stable — otherwise every new forge touches the router. Canonical names become
943	neutral (`explorer` is already an alias and becomes the name; `auth` for the
944	other), and `gitlab-auth` / `gla` **and** `github-auth` / `gha` all parse, to the
945	same view.
946	
947	Deliberately permissive: there is only one authentication view, so `gla` typed
948	in a GitHub context should go there rather than fail. Punishing muscle memory
949	buys nothing. **The filtering happens in completion, not in parsing** — `gla`
950	always works, but is never *suggested* while the active forge is GitHub. That
951	split is what makes it feel fluid without breaking anything existing.
952	
953	Messages that quote a command (`explorer/view.go:258`,
954	`dashboard/view.go:85`) must quote the active forge's spelling; once the
955	vocabulary is centralised that is one more field on the same struct.
956	
957	**Forge selection: detect, and let the user take it back.** URL sniffing alone is
958	unreliable — `github.com` and `gitlab.com` are trivial, but self-hosted is the
959	case that matters and `git.acme.com` could be either. Probing (`/api/v4/version`
960	vs `/api/v3/`) costs a round-trip and fails on instances that require auth on
961	those endpoints. A mandatory picker alone is friction on the two most common
962	cases, where the URL is unambiguous. So:
963	
964	- The forge is **field 0** of the auth form, above the URL. It governs the URL
965	  placeholder, the token placeholder and label, and the scope help — putting it
966	  first is what lets everything below it reconfigure live.
967	- It is a **cycle field** (`←` / `→`, Rule 132), pre-filled by host detection.
968	- Detection re-runs as the URL is typed, **but only while the user has not
969	  touched the forge field** — a dirty flag. Without it, detection overwrites an
970	  explicit choice, which is the difference between helpful and possessive.
971	- The token prefix (`glpat-` vs `ghp_` / `github_pat_`) is a second signal used
972	  to **warn**, never to switch: by then the user has already chosen above.
973	- **Once authentication succeeds the forge is frozen for that context**, per the
974	  one-forge-per-context decision. Changing it requires an explicit logout, or a
975	  new context. Before a successful login it stays freely editable.
976	
977	This makes the auth form mix a cycle field with the radio buttons it uses for
978	the save options (`auth/view.go:146`) — themselves a closed two-value set, so
979	the form was already at odds with Rule 132. **Settled in §3.9**: those radios are
980	deleted outright, along with the choice they present, so the form is left with a
981	cycle field and nothing else.
982	
983	#### Open decision: Go SDKs or the `gh` / `glab` CLIs
984	
985	Worth deciding before any code is written, because it determines whether the
986	package needs a seam.
987	
988	Arguments for the CLIs:
989	
990	- Authentication is already solved, including OAuth device flow, self-hosted
991	  hosts and token storage. DevDesk's own credential handling could shrink — and
992	  it has already proven fragile (see §1.1).
993	- `gh api` and `glab api` are raw REST/GraphQL passthroughs, so no SDK is needed
994	  for coverage of endpoints the abstraction does not model.
995	- No SDK version churn to track for two forges.
996	
997	Arguments against:
998	
999	- **Per-context isolation conflicts with how these tools store auth.** Both keep
1000	  global per-host state (`~/.config/gh/hosts.yml`). DevDesk contexts want
1001	  *different tokens for the same host*. Driving `gh auth switch` from the TUI
1002	  would mutate the user's global CLI state — the exact mistake avoided in §1.1 by
1003	  scoping `credential.useHttpPath` to the invocation. The clean route is
1004	  `GH_TOKEN` / `GITLAB_TOKEN` per invocation, but then DevDesk still owns the
1005	  tokens and the main benefit is gone.
1006	- **Two more hard dependencies.** Today DevDesk needs `git`, and `docker` only
1007	  for the features that use it. Requiring `gh` and `glab` for the core forge
1008	  feature is a real setup-friction regression.
1009	- **Cost per call.** A process spawn per request, against a reused HTTP
1010	  connection today. The dashboard alone issues five calls, and the explorer
1011	  paginates.
1012	- **Testability regresses.** `internal/gitlab` reaches 100 % with no seam,
1013	  because the SDK takes a base URL that an `httptest` server can stand in for.
1014	  Shelling out would put it back in the position `internal/docker` was in, needing
1015	  a manufactured seam — and stubbed CLI output encodes assumptions about the tool
1016	  rather than testing against it.
1017	
1018	**Current recommendation:** keep Go SDKs (go-gitlab, go-github) for the API
1019	surface, and use the CLIs only as an *optional* token source — when a context has
1020	no token, offer to read one from `gh auth token --hostname <host>` or
1021	`glab auth status`. That takes the convenience without the coupling. Recorded as
1022	a recommendation, not a decision.
1023	
1024	#### Sketch of the work
1025	
1026	0. Collapse the four command tables into one source, and let `Parse`,
1027	   `GetAliases` and `buildCommands` derive from it. Independent of everything
1028	   else, and it fixes the stale completion list today.
1029	1. Define a `forge` abstraction from what the code actually consumes: current
1030	   user, namespace tree, create/delete namespace and repository, initial commit,
1031	   dashboard counters, clone URL. It also declares its **shape** — depth,
1032	   visibility set, humanised roles — not just its data.
1033	2. Replace `shared.State.GitLabClient` with that interface, and switch the
1034	   authenticated-or-not branches to `IsAuthenticated` while passing through.
1035	   This is the change the other 65 call sites follow from.
1036	3. Generalise `GitLabConfig` into a per-context forge config carrying a
1037	   `type: gitlab | github` discriminator, and migrate existing config files.
1038	4. Extract the `Vocabulary` table and move every literal in the table above onto
1039	   it, with the grep test that keeps them from coming back. Doable against
1040	   GitLab alone, before any GitHub code exists — which is what makes it a
1041	   refactor rather than a rewrite.

# DevDesk Backlog

**Last Updated:** 2026-08-03

Open work for DevDesk: known defects, technical debt, and planned features.
Replaces the former `todo.md` at the repository root. Items completed there
(network topology visualisation, inter-container ping/curl) have been dropped
rather than carried over.

---

## 1. Known defects

**Three open**, all in the registry browser and all found while reviewing the
design for §3.8 rather than by a test. See [§1.3](#13-open). D1–D11 and D15–D19
are fixed; §1.1 records what each was and why the chosen fix was the right one.

The five that stayed open longest — D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 — were parked not
because they were hard but because each altered something the user already saw,
so they needed a deliberate call rather than a drive-by fix. All five were then
decided together and fixed in one pass; see [§1.2](#12-the-five-parked-defects).

### 1.1 Fixed

**The command line took focus from the render path.** Found in phase 5.
`renderHeader` called `a.commandInput.Focus()` whenever `commandMode` was set —
a mutation inside `View()`, which Rule 110 makes read-only. A
`bubbles/textinput` drops every key it receives while blurred, so the command
line only accepted typing because a render happened to have run first. Focus is
now taken in `enterCommandMode` and released alongside the existing `Blur()`
calls on the way out. In production the ordering held, so nothing was visibly
broken; the coupling surfaced the moment a test drove the router without
rendering, and the same latent bug would bite anyone reordering the loop.

**Two views' help advertised keys that do nothing.** Found while writing the
phase 2 tests, not previously recorded.

The status view's `GetHelpContent` documented `n` for "Add a new monitor" while
the binding has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111 standardised it, and the `/` filter
was missing altogether; the empty-state message told the user to "Press [n]" too.
The containers view advertised `S` (shell in a new window) in `GetShortcuts()`
without documenting it at all.

The workspaces view had it too, found in phase 3: `n` and `Enter` documented
where the bindings are `ctrl+n` and `enter`, `/` undocumented, and the same
stale "Press [n]" in its empty state.

`explorer` made it four in a row, though only just: every key was documented
except `/`. The check caught it on its first run.

`security` broke the streak — its help documents every key its header
advertises, across all four states.

`oci_resources` then produced the worst instance, in phase 4. The Networks and
Volumes tabs documented `n` for a binding that has been `ctrl+n` since Rule 111
renamed it — the same drift `status` and `workspaces` carried — but the **whole
Registries tab was undocumented**: `ctrl+n`, `e`, `l` and `L` appeared nowhere,
so four actions on a tab were reachable only by guessing.

That view needed one adjustment to the check: its help qualifies most keys with
the tab they belong to (`enter (Images)`, `ctrl+n (Networks)`), so the
parenthetical comes off before matching. That convention is worth keeping — with
four tabs sharing a keymap, an unqualified `enter` would be ambiguous.

So the pattern across five views: the drift is a Rule 111 rename the help did
not follow, plus whole surfaces added later and never documented at all.

All five are fixed, and every view in `internal/ui` now asserts that each key
`GetShortcuts()` advertises appears in `GetHelpContent()` — the check that would
have caught the drift when it was introduced.

**The explorer acted on a different row than the one highlighted.** Found in
phase 3, and the most serious defect the coverage work has turned up.

`handleKeyMsg` resolved the cursor against `sortedItems(currentItems())` — the
unfiltered list — while the table was built from the filtered one. With a filter
active the two indices disagree, so `ctrl+d`, `p`, `→` and `ctrl+w` all acted on
whatever happened to sit at that index in the *unfiltered* list. Filtering to a
single project and pressing `ctrl+d` scheduled a different group for deletion.
`GetShortcuts` had it too, so even the advertised `ctrl+w` keyed off the wrong
node.

Both now go through `visibleItems()`, the single list `updateTableRows` builds
from. Pinned by `TestActionsResolveTheRowTheUserCanSee`, which filters to a row
that sits at a different index in each list — the fixtures were chosen so the
two cannot coincide.

**A stranded cursor in the workspaces table.** `bubbles/table.SetRows` does not
clamp the cursor when the row count shrinks. Drilling into a directory with
fewer entries — or narrowing the filter — left the cursor past the end: nothing
highlighted, and `enter`, `ctrl+d`, `r` and `ctrl+s` all silently did nothing
until the user pressed an arrow key. `updateTableData` now clamps.

The containers view avoids this by calling `GotoTop()` after every filter
change; workspaces had no equivalent. **`explorer` had it too**, and only on the
filter path — its drill-down was already safe because it calls `GotoTop()`.
Fixed the same way.

**Two tabs reported nothing when Docker was down.** Found in phase 4.
`handleImagesList` has always set a footer message on failure;
`handleNetworksList` and `handleVolumesList` only logged, so with the daemon
stopped those two tabs showed an empty table — indistinguishable from "you have
no networks". Both now match their sibling.

**The Registries tab opened empty.** `switchTab` focused the table and fired the
`docker login` status check, but never called `updateRegistryTable()` — so the
tab stayed blank until an asynchronous Docker call answered, even though the
registries come from the config file and were available immediately.

**A search counter with no floor.** `RegistryBrowser.AddRegistryTags`
decremented `pendingSearches` unconditionally. A duplicate or late response drove
it negative, and the *next* search then started from that base: `IsSearching()`
stayed false while requests were genuinely in flight, so the spinner never
showed. Floored at zero.

**Footer messages with no timer.** `explorer.handleDeleteComplete` set
`footerError` and returned `nil`, so a failed delete left "Delete failed — check
logs" on screen until something else overwrote it. Rule 128 caps footer messages
at three seconds, and the same file's `BrowserOpenedMsg` handler already did it
correctly. Now returns `clearFooterErrorCmd()`.

The security view had it worse: **Rule 128 was not honoured anywhere in it.**
`statusMessage` was set in three places — "Added x to .gitleaksignore", "Failed
to ignore secret", "No references available" — and there was no clear timer in
the package at all, so whichever happened last stayed on screen until a tab
switch happened to reset it. `clearStatusCmd` / `clearStatusMsg` added and all
three wired, pinned by `TestFooterMessagesExpire`.

**D7** (`extractTarGz` kept parent references in archive paths), **D2** (the
"permanent delete" checkbox was documented as locked but was not) and **D5** (an
unreachable focus clamp in `CreationForm`) were fixed together — three small,
independent defects with no shared code.

`extractTarGz` now routes every member name through `sanitizeArchivePath`, which
normalises the separators and rejects anything resolving outside the root.
Cleaning happens *after* the leading separator is stripped, not before:
`path.Clean("/../x")` returns `"/x"`, which would have absorbed the traversal
silently instead of exposing it. Traversal that resolves back inside the root
(`templates/../README.md`) is kept, normalised. Backslashes are folded to `/`
first, so `..\..\etc\passwd` cannot pass as an ordinary filename on a tar reader
that treats it as one.

The delete modal carries a `locked` flag, set only by
`NewDeleteConfirmModalPermanent`. Rather than merely making the toggle a no-op,
navigation skips the checkbox entirely (`minFocus()` / `cycleFocus()`) and the
line renders dimmed: a focusable control that ignores every key is more
confusing than one that is plainly not there.

The `CreationForm` clamp was deleted and replaced by a comment recording why it
cannot fire, so it is not reintroduced defensively. A test pins the invariant it
was guarding.

Both self-annulling tests became real assertions:
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsStillToggleable` →
`TestDeleteConfirmModalPermanentCheckboxIsLocked` (plus navigation and
confirmation cases), and `TestExtractTarGzPreservesParentTraversalInKeys` →
`TestExtractTarGzRejectsParentTraversal` (table-driven over five escape shapes)
alongside `TestExtractTarGzNormalisesContainedTraversal`.

**D1** (`ReportModal.View()` emitted invalid UTF-8), **D3** (`wrapInputLines`
looped forever when `wrapWidth <= 0`) and **D6** (`wordWrap` measured bytes) were
fixed together, since D1 and D6 were the same byte-vs-rune defect.

Rather than patch each call site, the truncation logic moved into
`internal/ui/theme/text.go` per Rule 117: `StringWidth`, `TruncateWidth` (keeps
the head) and `TruncateTailWidth` (keeps the tail, for paths). All three measure
terminal columns, so double-width glyphs are handled too, not just multibyte
ones.

A **fourth site carried the same defect** and was not recorded here: `truncate`
in `internal/ui/security/model.go` sliced bytes exactly like D1 and rendered
Trivy finding titles. It is now `theme.TruncateWidth` and the local helper is
gone.

A **sixth site** closed the family out, in the last package of phase 3:
`parseVersion` in `internal/ui/security` truncated its fallback with
`result[:15]`. Version strings are ASCII in practice, so this was the
lowest-risk of the six — but it is the same pattern, and it is now
`theme.TruncateWidth`. Grepping for `[:` on strings across `internal/ui` now
returns nothing but slice indexing.

The same function had a second defect: it scanned for the version number by
taking the first whitespace-separated token starting with `v`, so
`gitleaks version 8.18.2` reported its version as **"version"**. A leading `v`
now only counts when a digit follows it.

A **fifth site** turned up during the phase 3 tests: `firstOutputLine` in
`internal/ui/netdiag` sliced `line[:maxLen-3]` to fill the Output column of the
results table, so any diagnostic whose first line contained a multibyte rune
could be cut in half and bleed across the rows below (Rule 122). Now
`theme.TruncateWidth`, pinned by `TestFirstOutputLineKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`.
Worth grepping for `[:` on strings when the remaining phases land.

The two pinned tests that `t.Skip()`d became real assertions
(`TestReportModalViewKeepsMultibyteRunesIntact`,
`TestWordWrapMeasuresColumnsNotBytes`).

One call site was deliberately left alone: `truncateResultLine` in
`internal/ui/oci_resources/connectivity_form.go` counts runes rather than bytes,
so it is correct — merely imprecise on double-width glyphs. Folding it into the
theme helpers is a cleanup, not a defect fix.

**Every scan came back empty.** Introduced by the `internal/scan` split itself
and caught within the hour by the coverage pass that followed it — the clearest
argument yet for the surface → split → cover order.

Extracting the subprocess seam collapsed two statements into one return:

```go
return stdout.Bytes(), waitErr(tc.Name, cmd.Wait(), stderr.String())
```

Operands are evaluated before the call, so `stdout.Bytes()` snapshots the buffer
**before** `cmd.Wait()` runs — and `os/exec` fills that buffer from goroutines
only Wait is guaranteed to have finished. `Bytes()` returns a slice header with
the length at that moment, so later writes are invisible: the report was always
empty, every scan reported no findings, and the exit code alone survived. The
code it replaced got this right by accident of being written as separate
statements.

The read now lives in `finish`, after Wait, with the reasoning recorded next to
it so it is not re-collapsed. Pinned by `TestTheReportOnStdoutIsWhatComesBack`,
which is the test that failed first when the seam was finally exercised.

Worth stating plainly: this is the one defect in this list that the tests
*introduced* rather than merely found, and it never reached a commit. A
mechanical-looking refactor changed evaluation order, which is exactly what a
package with no tests under it cannot tell you.

**Context isolation in `GitCredentialStorage` never worked.** Found while
planning the coverage work, not previously recorded.

The three methods carried the DevDesk context in the `path` field of the git
credential protocol (`path=devdesk/context/<name>`). Git discards that field
unless `credential.useHttpPath` is set, which is off by default, so every
credential was keyed on `protocol://host` alone. Two contexts pointing at the
same GitLab host silently overwrote each other, and the last one to authenticate
won for all of them. Verified against a real `git credential` store before and
after the fix; it affects every helper (GCM, wincred, osxkeychain), since git
strips the path before the helper is ever called.

**Fix:** pass `-c credential.useHttpPath=true` on each invocation. Scoping it to
the call leaves the user's git configuration alone — setting it globally would
change credential resolution for every repository on the machine. Pinned by
`TestGitCredentialIsolatesContexts`.

Existing users must re-authenticate: credentials saved under the old
path-stripped key no longer match. Those credentials were ambiguous across
contexts anyway.

Two smaller defects went with it:

- `Delete` had no timeout, while `Save` and `Load` bounded themselves to 2 s
  precisely so an unconfigured helper could not freeze the TUI. Logout could
  hang indefinitely.
- The timeout killed only the direct `git` child, though its comment claimed
  otherwise. The helper git spawns survives and holds the output pipes open, so
  `Run` kept blocking. All three calls now share one `runCredential` helper built
  on `exec.CommandContext` plus `WaitDelay`, which bounds the wait on those pipes.

`internal/credentials/helper.go` (`HelperStorage`, 137 lines) was deleted rather
than fixed: nothing outside its own tests constructed it. It was also broken —
`detectHelper()` returns whatever `git config credential.helper` holds, so a
common value like `store --file=/path` became the single unfindable command
`credential-store --file=/path` — and it hardcoded `protocol=https`, unlike
`GitCredentialStorage`, which reads the scheme from the URL.

**D15 — `esc` never reached a view that was not editing.** The router answered
`esc` itself through `maybeQuitCommandMode`, forwarding it only when the view
reported `InEditMode()`. Every esc-to-go-back handler behind that gate was dead
code: the explorer's `esc` → `handleDrillUp` could not fire, though Rule 111
lists `esc` as the third way up.

**Fix:** the router no longer names `esc` at all — it falls through to the
default branch and is forwarded like any other key. What made this smaller than
it looked is that the router had nothing left to do with `esc` by the time the
branch ran: `handleCommandMode` answers first whenever the command line is open,
so `maybeQuitCommandMode` was resetting an already-closed line and asking for a
redundant resize. It is deleted.

The interesting half is what the gate had done to the views. Two of them
declared themselves *editing* in states holding no field at all, for one reason
— it was the only way to be handed `esc`. The security view said so outright:
`InEditMode()` was documented as *"returns true when the view needs to handle
ESC key"*, and claimed `StateScanning`, `StateResults` and `StateDetails`;
netdiag claimed `StateRunning` and `StateDetails`. That claim costs more than it
buys, because `InEditMode()` also governs `:`, `q` and `?` — so the security
results screen, the one place a user most wants to jump elsewhere, was the one
place `:` did nothing. Both predicates are now about focus and nothing else, and
those states get the command line, the help overlay and quit back.

Left alone deliberately: the containers view claims `stateLogs`, where `q`
really is the view's own key for leaving the log pane. That is key ownership,
not a workaround for `esc`.

**D16 — `:netdiag` was documented but not accepted.** One missing map entry.
**D17 — the completion catalogue was a subset of the parser.** Eight commands
listed against fourteen views plus aliases, kept by hand in two places.

**Fix, for both:** one map. `viewNames` in `parser.go` maps every accepted
spelling to its view, the key equal to the `ViewType` being the full name and
every other key an alias; `GetAliases()` and the new `FullNames()` derive from
it, and the completion engine derives from those. Two tests hold the two ends
together — everything the parser accepts is suggested, everything suggested
parses — so the lists cannot drift apart again. `ParseCommand` lost its chain of
`if mainCmd ==` comparisons to the same treatment, `actionNames` and
`actionAliases`, and `Parse` is now a lookup in `viewNames` rather than a third
copy of it.

Two aliases documented in `CLAUDE.md` but accepted nowhere came out of this —
`gle` for the explorer and `w` for workspaces — the same defect as D16, found by
the test rather than by reading. `ViewNet` was renamed `ViewNetdiag` and its
value changed from `net` to `netdiag`, so the full name matches the view, the
package and the documentation; `net` remains an alias.

**D18 — the header overflowed a narrow window.** `buildShortcutLines` meant to
clip the shortcut block to its column — the comment said *"Truncate if wider
than col2Width"* — but called `theme.PadWithBg`, which returns content untouched
once it is already at or past the target. Below roughly 100 columns the header
rendered wider than the window and wrapped, costing the viewport a row.

**Fix:** `lipgloss.NewStyle().MaxWidth(col2Width)`, which truncates on rune
boundaries without cutting an escape sequence in half — the corruption Rule 122
is about. Width 80 is now part of `TestEveryHeaderRowFillsTheWidth`, and a
second test checks no row ends inside an escape sequence, which is the failure a
naive slice would have produced.

### 1.2 The five parked defects

D4, D8, D9, D10 and D11 were each recorded rather than fixed on discovery,
because each changed something the user already saw. They were decided together
and fixed in one pass. Three of the five had a test written to fail *on the
fix*, and all three did.

**D4 — `tab` navigated the delete confirmation.** Rule 135 reserves `tab` for
switching tabs and assigns field navigation to `↑ / ↓` exclusively; the modal
had it exactly inverted, cycling on `tab` and clamping on `↑ / ↓`. `↑ / ↓` now
cycle, which is what keeps every control reachable in one direction, and the
`tab` cases are gone. The explorer no longer advertises "tab Navigate" while the
modal is open, and `↑↓` is not advertised in its place — Rule 138 calls it
obvious. The permanent variant still skips its locked checkbox, so cycling there
toggles between the two buttons.

**D8 — write-only CRUD flags.** `creating`, `editing` and `confirming` were
assigned in five places and read in none, and `ComponentFormCancelledMsg` — the
only thing that would have reset two of them — could never be sent. Deleted, all
of it. Nothing else changed: the phase 2 tests had deliberately asserted on
`componentForm` / `confirmModal` rather than on the flags, which is what made
this safe a phase later.

**D9 — the containers list opened Z→A.** `New()` set neither `sortColumn` nor
`sortAsc`, so both took their zero value. Both are now set explicitly, so the
default is stated rather than inherited. `TestDefaultSortIsNameDescending`
became `TestDefaultSortIsNameAscending`, and the cycle test walks forward from
ascending. The `loadedModel` helper still sets the sort itself even though it
now matches the constructor: those tests should say which order they rely on.

**D10 — a registry failure was invisible.** `renderTemplateList` returned early
when the field was unfocused and the warning sat below that return, so a form
opened after the OCI registry failed offered a Template field reading "none"
with nothing to distinguish "the registry is down" from "there are no
templates". The warning moved into `renderTemplateWarning` and is appended in
both branches — it explains why the list is empty, so it belongs wherever the
list is.

**D11 — CRITICAL and HIGH rendered identically.** `getSeverityStyle` composed
CRITICAL by hand as `ColorError` + `Bold`, which is byte-for-byte the
`theme.StatusErrorStyle` it returned for HIGH. The palette moved to
`theme.SeverityTextStyle`, next to the `TableStylesForSeverity` it draws from,
and the view delegates (Rule 102). An unrecognised severity now falls back to
the info colour rather than to `DimStyle`, so it is still legible.

The pattern worth keeping: when a defect is recorded rather than fixed, write
the test **inverted** — asserting the current behaviour and saying so. D9, D10
and D11 each had one, and each failed the moment the fix landed, which is how
the stale test and the stale backlog entry got found together.

### 1.3 Open

D12–D14 sit in `internal/ui/oci_resources` and are cheap on their own, but
§3.8 rewrites the code path each of them lives in. Fix them **as part of** that
work rather than ahead of it, and write each one's test inverted first, per the
pattern above.

D15–D19 were found by the phase 5 pass, were unrelated to §3.8, and are fixed —
see §1.1. Each had been recorded with an inverted test asserting the broken
behaviour; those tests are what failed when the fix landed, and each has been
turned around to assert the fixed behaviour instead.

**D12 — `AuthEnabled` has no effect on browse or discovery.** The flag is
honoured in exactly three places: the `docker login` fired on form submit, the
`Logged` column, and the URL list `registryLoginStatusCmd` checks. Neither code
path that actually talks to a registry consults it. `submitSearch`
(`browser_keys.go:142`) calls `docker.GetStoredCreds(credURL)`
unconditionally and hands the result to `searchRegistryTagsCmd`;
`detectRegistryGroupCmd` (`commands.go:563`) does the same before calling into
`registrymgr`. A registry the user has marked as needing no authentication will
still have the host's stored credentials sent to it whenever any other registry
on that host has been logged into — which, given that Docker keys credentials by
host, is the normal case for a Nexus instance. This is the defect the
`anonymous` mode in §3.8 exists to make expressible; today there is no way to
say "do not send credentials here" at all.

**D13 — the browser cannot be dismissed while it is resolving.**
`handleKeyMsg` returns `nil` for every key in `browserStateResolving`
(`browser_keys.go:70`), `esc` included, and that state is entered
unconditionally on open whenever any registry is configured. The detections run
concurrently with an 8 s timeout each, so the wedge is bounded at roughly eight
seconds — but it is eight seconds during which the application ignores the user,
on a screen they may have opened by mistake. §3.8 removes the state rather than
the symptom: with members read from config and cache, there is nothing to
resolve and the form renders immediately.

A smaller thing in the same handler, not worth its own entry:
`HandleGroupDetected` matches the incoming result against `reg.URL`, so two
registries configured with the same URL collide and the second result overwrites
the first. The slug introduced in §3.8 is the natural key to match on instead.

**D14 — the registry filter shows a raw URL for group members.**
`registryFilterLabel()` (`browser_tags.go:63`) resolves the active filter by
searching `b.registries`, which holds only the configured top-level entries.
Discovered members are not in that list, so filtering to one falls through to
returning `b.registryFilter` — the full synthesised URL — where every other row
in the same view shows a short alias. The fix follows from §3.8 rather than
preceding it: once members are persisted they are resolvable, and the filter
gains a group level at the same time.

Two techniques from it are reusable:

- **The test binary stands in for the tool.** `TestMain` notices a set of

  does — a report on stdout, progress on stderr, a chosen exit code. That is what
  covers the *production* runner (`cliRunner`) rather than only the code above

- **Detection is steered through `PATH`.** `CheckDependenciesWithImages` probes
  the machine, which is precisely what a test must not do. Copying the test
  binary into `t.TempDir()` as `trivy`, `gitleaks` or `docker` and pointing

  over image, image absent, daemon unreachable, version unreadable. A per-argument
  refusal knob is what separates `docker images` from `docker run` when both are
  the same fake.

branches are worth.

"editing" hostage, which no view could have reported on its own either.

### Race detector cannot run locally

`mise run test-race` needs cgo and therefore a C compiler on `PATH`. Without one
it fails with `cgo: C compiler "gcc" not found`. Bubble Tea `Cmd`s run
concurrently, so this is the check most likely to catch a Rule 110 violation.

**Now covered by CI.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs `mise run test-race` on
every push and pull request, on `ubuntu-latest`, which has a toolchain. The first
run reported no data race across all 17 packages.

That is a baseline, not a clean bill of health: the detector only sees code the
tests actually execute, and coverage is 73.6 %. Rule 110 violations in untested
paths remain invisible. The two efforts compound, so this is an argument for the
coverage phases rather than a substitute for them.

`internal/scan` is the package the detector has most to say about, since
`Scanner.Scan` is the only place in the application that fans out to concurrent
goroutines writing one shared result. Its tests now drive all five stages at
once, so that fan-out is under the detector for the first time — but only on CI,
which is where the confirmation has to be read.

Installing a local toolchain is still worth doing for anyone touching `Cmd`s, to
avoid learning about a race from CI after the fact.
